mitigations.primitive_impact: No stack canary. This primitive does not overwrite the canary (it's a 1-byte read, not write), so canary absence is not relevant to this primitive.

mitigations.name: No PIE
mitigations.primitive_impact: No PIE means code/rodata addresses are fixed. This primitive reads 1 byte of stack data that is never leaked to the attacker, so PIE/ASLR status is not relevant.

mitigations.name: Partial RELRO
mitigations.primitive_impact: Partial RELRO allows GOT writes. This primitive is a 1-byte stack read, not a GOT write, so RELRO is not relevant.

evidence.description: read() return value stored at [rbp-0x4] (0x40123e), then eax = [rbp-0x4] - 1 (0x401244), cdqe sign-extends (0x401247), movzx eax, BYTE PTR [rbp+rax*1-0x70] (0x401249). No check for read() returning <= 0 before using as index.

GDB verification: When stdin reaches EOF, second read() returns rax=0. At movzx (0x401249): rax=0xffffffffffffffff (sign-extended -1), rbp=0x7fffffffeb30, buffer start (rbp-0x70)=0x7fffffffeac0, OOB access addr=0x7fffffffeabf (rbp-0x71), offset from buffer start = -1 bytes (BELOW buffer). Byte read at OOB addr = 0x00. Byte != 0x0a → no OOB write. No crash (address is mapped stack).

GDB stack layout: [rbp-0x78]=0x4e (init 'N'), [rbp-0x71]=0x00 (init high bytes of QWORD 0x4e), [rbp-0x70]=0x41 (buffer start, 'A' from first read). The OOB byte at rbp-0x71 is always 0x00 because: (1) init sets QWORD[rbp-0x78]=0x4e → rbp-0x71=0x00, (2) scanf(%7s) never writes 0x0a (whitespace stops %s), (3) in practice scanf gets EOF (read consumes all stdin) so field retains init value.

The OOB read value (0x00) is compared to 0x0a at 0x40124e. Since 0x00 != 0x0a, the conditional OOB write at 0x40125a (mov BYTE PTR [rbp+rax*1-0x70], 0x0) is NOT executed. The read value is never output to the attacker (printf uses the buffer content, not the OOB byte). No information leak occurs.

verification_result.details: GDB dynamic verification confirmed: when read() returns 0 (EOF), rax=0xffffffffffffffff at movzx (0x401249), OOB access at rbp-0x71 (0x7fffffffeabf), byte read=0x00, no crash, no write triggered. The OOB read value is only used for comparison with 0x0a and is never leaked to the attacker. PoC at poc-BUG-002.py uses GDB to set breakpoints and observe the OOB read.

primitives.notes: PRIM-001 is a very weak primitive: a 1-byte OOB read below the stack buffer, where the read value (0x00) is only used for a newline comparison and is never output to the attacker. No information leak, no memory corruption, no crash. The OOB address (rbp-0x71) is always within the mapped stack frame. This is a low-severity issue with minimal exploit value. The read-returns-(-1) path (accessing rbp-0x72) is not practically triggerable via normal stdin operation.

source.root_cause: SIGNEDNESS_ERROR: Same as PRIM-001. After the OOB read at 0x401249, if the read byte equals 0x0a (newline), the code writes a NUL byte at the same OOB address: mov BYTE PTR [rbp+rax*1-0x70], 0x0 at 0x40125a. This is a conditional OOB write of a single NUL byte.
source.description: If the byte at the OOB address (rbp-0x71 when read returns 0, or rbp-0x72 when read returns -1) happens to be 0x0a, the code writes 0x00 (NUL) at that same OOB address. This would be a 1-byte OOB write of a NUL byte.

chain: BUG-002
SIGNEDNESS_ERROR: read() return value used as index without checking for <= 0
read() returns 0 (EOF) → eax = -1 → cdqe → rax = 0xffffffffffffffff → OOB read at rbp-0x71
If byte at rbp-0x71 == 0x0a: mov BYTE PTR [rbp+rax*1-0x70], 0x0 → OOB write of NUL at rbp-0x71
RESTRICTED_WRITE: conditional 1-byte NUL write at OOB offset (THEORETICAL — cannot trigger)

controlled_element.what: Nothing controllable. The OOB write only occurs if the byte at the OOB address is 0x0a, but the attacker cannot control this byte.
controlled_element.how: The byte at rbp-0x71 is set by initialization (0x00) or scanf's NUL terminator (0x00). scanf %s never writes 0x0a (whitespace stops matching). The read() call writes to rbp-0x70 and above, not to rbp-0x71. Therefore the attacker has no way to place 0x0a at the OOB address.

preconditions.description: read() must return 0 (EOF) or -1 (error) to trigger the OOB access. read returning 0 is achievable via stdin EOF. read returning -1 requires an error condition (e.g. EBADF) not achievable via normal stdin.
preconditions.necessity: Without a non-positive read return value, no OOB access occurs.

preconditions.description: The byte at the OOB address (rbp-0x71 for read=0, rbp-0x72 for read=-1) must equal 0x0a (newline) to trigger the NUL write. Analysis shows this byte is always 0x00: (a) initialization sets QWORD[rbp-0x78]=0x4e → rbp-0x71=0x00, rbp-0x72=0x00; (b) scanf(%7s) never writes 0x0a; (c) in practice scanf gets EOF so the field retains init values.
preconditions.necessity: Without the byte being 0x0a, the conditional write branch (jne at 0x401250) is taken and no write occurs.

preconditions.description: Even if the write were triggered, it would write 0x00 (NUL) to rbp-0x71, which already contains 0x00. The write would have no observable memory effect.
preconditions.necessity: For the primitive to have any impact, the written value must differ from the existing value. Since both are 0x00, no effect occurs.

alias_key_findings.expression: rbp-0x71 (OOB write target when read returns 0)
alias_key_findings.alias: rbp-0x71 is the highest byte of the QWORD at [rbp-0x78] (scanf continue_flag field). Init = 0x00. scanf NUL terminator (if 7 chars) = 0x00. scanf %s never writes 0x0a. In practice scanf gets EOF so field retains init value.
alias_key_findings.implication: The byte at rbp-0x71 is always 0x00, never 0x0a. The conditional OOB write cannot be triggered via read returning 0. Even if it could, writing 0x00 to a location that already contains 0x00 has no effect.

alias_key_findings.expression: rbp-0x72 (OOB write target when read returns -1)
alias_key_findings.alias: rbp-0x72 is the 7th byte of [rbp-0x78]. Init = 0x00. scanf 7th char (if 7 chars) — but %s never writes 0x0a. scanf NUL terminator (if 6 chars) = 0x00.
alias_key_findings.implication: rbp-0x72 is also never 0x0a. The read-returns-(-1) path is not practically triggerable anyway. OOB write cannot be triggered.

verification_plan.method: Static analysis + GDB dynamic verification of the byte values at the OOB addresses. GDB confirmed rbp-0x71 = 0x00 and rbp-0x72 = 0x00 at runtime. Since the conditional write requires the byte to be 0x0a, and the byte is always 0x00, the write path is never taken.
verification_plan.environment: Linux x86-64, glibc 2.39, No PIE, No canary, Partial RELRO, NX enabled
expected_evidence: Conditional write branch (jne at 0x401250) is always taken (byte != 0x0a)

mitigations.name: NX
mitigations.primitive_impact: NX prevents code execution from stack. This primitive is a 1-byte NUL write, not code execution. Not directly relevant.

mitigations.name: No Canary
mitigations.primitive_impact: No stack canary. This primitive writes to rbp-0x71 (below the buffer, not near the canary position). Not relevant.

evidence.description: cmp al, 0x0a (0x40124e); jne 0x40125f (0x401250, skip write if not newline); mov BYTE PTR [rbp+rax*1-0x70], 0x0 (0x40125a, OOB NUL write). The write only occurs if the OOB-read byte equals 0x0a.

GDB confirmed: byte at rbp-0x71 (OOB address when read returns 0) = 0x00. Since 0x00 != 0x0a, the jne at 0x401250 is taken and the OOB write at 0x40125a is NOT executed. The byte at rbp-0x71 is always 0x00 because: init sets QWORD[rbp-0x78]=0x4e (rbp-0x71=0x00), scanf %s never writes 0x0a, and in practice scanf gets EOF so the field retains init values.

Even if the OOB write were triggered (byte == 0x0a), it would write 0x00 to rbp-0x71, which already contains 0x00. The write would have no observable memory effect. The primitive is theoretically possible in the code path but practically untriggerable and has no impact even if triggered.

verification_result.read_value: 0x00 (byte at OOB address, not 0x0a, so write not triggered)
verification_result.details: GDB verification confirmed the byte at the OOB address (rbp-0x71) is 0x00, not 0x0a. The conditional write path (mov BYTE PTR [rbp+rax-0x70], 0x0 at 0x40125a) is never executed because the jne at 0x401250 always takes the branch (byte != 0x0a). The OOB write is theoretically present in the code but cannot be triggered because the attacker cannot place 0x0a at the OOB address.

primitives.notes: PRIM-002 is a theoretical primitive: the code path for an OOB NUL byte write exists (0x40125a), but it cannot be triggered because: (1) the byte at the OOB address is always 0x00 (from initialization or scanf NUL terminator), (2) scanf %s never writes 0x0a (whitespace stops matching), (3) read() writes to rbp-0x70 and above, not to rbp-0x71/0x72. Even if triggered, writing 0x00 to a location already containing 0x00 has no effect. This is a dead-end primitive with no exploit value.

non_primitives.reason: The OOB access addresses (rbp-0x71 when read returns 0, rbp-0x72 when read returns -1) are always within the mapped stack frame (frame spans rbp-0x80 to rbp). GDB confirmed no SIGSEGV occurs — the program continues looping normally after the OOB read. A crash would require the OOB address to be unmapped, which is impossible for offsets of -1 and -2 from the buffer within the stack frame.

The OOB read value (1 byte at rbp-0x71) is only used for comparison with 0x0a (newline check at 0x40124e). It is never output to the attacker via printf or any other output function. printf("%s", rbp-0x70) prints the buffer content, not the OOB byte. No information is leaked through this primitive.

The OOB read address is not attacker-controlled. It is always rbp-0x71 (when read returns 0) or rbp-0x72 (when read returns -1) — fixed offsets from rbp determined by the read return value. The attacker can only choose between offset -1 (read returns 0) and offset -2 (read returns -1), both of which are fixed relative to the stack frame. This is a RESTRICTED_READ (1 byte at a fixed negative offset), not an ARB_READ.

unresolved.description: Whether read() can return -1 (error) in any practical scenario
unresolved.reason: read(0, buf, 0x100) returns -1 only on error (e.g. EBADF if fd 0 is invalid). In normal program execution with stdin as fd 0, this does not occur. It might be triggerable if the attacker could close fd 0 and reopen it as something else, but this requires an existing primitive to manipulate file descriptors, which is not available from BUG-002 alone.
unresolved.required_next_step: Not required for S3. The read-returns-(-1) path accesses rbp-0x72 (also always 0x00), so even if triggered, the outcome is identical to the read-returns-0 path: a 1-byte OOB read of 0x00, no write, no crash.
